     1	==========
     2	Unit tests
     3	==========
     4	
     5	Django comes with a test suite of its own, in the ``tests`` directory of the
     6	code base. It's our policy to make sure all tests pass at all times.
     7	
     8	We appreciate any and all contributions to the test suite!
     9	
    10	The Django tests all use the testing infrastructure that ships with Django for
    11	testing applications. See :doc:`/topics/testing/overview` for an explanation of
    12	how to write new tests.
    13	
    14	.. _running-unit-tests:
    15	
    16	Running the unit tests
    17	======================
    18	
    19	Quickstart
    20	----------
    21	
    22	First, `fork Django on GitHub <https://github.com/django/django/fork>`__.
    23	
    24	Second, create and activate a virtual environment. If you're not familiar with
    25	how to do that, read our :doc:`contributing tutorial </intro/contributing>`.
    26	
    27	Next, clone your fork, install some requirements, and run the tests:
    28	
    29	.. console::
    30	
    31	   $ git clone https://github.com/YourGitHubName/django.git django-repo
    32	   $ cd django-repo/tests
    33	   $ python -m pip install -e ..
    34	   $ python -m pip install -r requirements/py3.txt
    35	   $ ./runtests.py
    36	
    37	Installing the requirements will likely require some operating system packages
    38	that your computer doesn't have installed. You can usually figure out which
    39	package to install by doing a web search for the last line or so of the error
    40	message. Try adding your operating system to the search query if needed.
    41	
    42	If you have trouble installing the requirements, you can skip that step. See
    43	:ref:`running-unit-tests-dependencies` for details on installing the optional
    44	test dependencies. If you don't have an optional dependency installed, the
    45	tests that require it will be skipped.
    46	
    47	Running the tests requires a Django settings module that defines the databases
    48	to use. To help you get started, Django provides and uses a sample settings
    49	module that uses the SQLite database. See :ref:`running-unit-tests-settings` to
    50	learn how to use a different settings module to run the tests with a different
    51	database.
    52	
    53	Having problems? See :ref:`troubleshooting-unit-tests` for some common issues.
    54	
    55	Running tests using ``tox``
    56	---------------------------
    57	
    58	`Tox <https://tox.wiki/>`_ is a tool for running tests in different virtual
    59	environments. Django includes a basic ``tox.ini`` that automates some checks
    60	that our build server performs on pull requests. To run the unit tests and
    61	other checks (such as :ref:`import sorting <coding-style-imports>`, the
    62	:ref:`documentation spelling checker <documentation-spelling-check>`, and
    63	:ref:`code formatting <coding-style-python>`), install and run the ``tox``
    64	command from any place in the Django source tree:
    65	
    66	.. console::
    67	
    68	    $ python -m pip install tox
    69	    $ tox
    70	
    71	By default, ``tox`` runs the test suite with the bundled test settings file for
    72	SQLite, ``black``, ``blacken-docs``, ``flake8``, ``isort``, and the
    73	documentation spelling checker. In addition to the system dependencies noted
    74	elsewhere in this documentation, the command ``python3`` must be on your path
    75	and linked to the appropriate version of Python. A list of default environments
    76	can be seen as follows:
    77	
    78	.. console::
    79	
    80	    $ tox -l
    81	    py3
    82	    black
    83	    blacken-docs
    84	    flake8>=3.7.0
    85	    docs
    86	    isort>=5.1.0
    87	
    88	Testing other Python versions and database backends
    89	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    90	
    91	In addition to the default environments, ``tox`` supports running unit tests
    92	for other versions of Python and other database backends. Since Django's test
    93	suite doesn't bundle a settings file for database backends other than SQLite,
    94	however, you must :ref:`create and provide your own test settings
    95	<running-unit-tests-settings>`. For example, to run the tests on Python 3.9
    96	using PostgreSQL:
    97	
    98	.. console::
    99	
   100	    $ tox -e py39-postgres -- --settings=my_postgres_settings
   101	
   102	This command sets up a Python 3.9 virtual environment, installs Django's
   103	test suite dependencies (including those for PostgreSQL), and calls
   104	``runtests.py`` with the supplied arguments (in this case,
   105	``--settings=my_postgres_settings``).
   106	
   107	The remainder of this documentation shows commands for running tests without
   108	``tox``, however, any option passed to ``runtests.py`` can also be passed to
   109	``tox`` by prefixing the argument list with ``--``, as above.
   110	
   111	``Tox`` also respects the :envvar:`DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` environment
   112	variable, if set. For example, the following is equivalent to the command
   113	above:
   114	
   115	.. code-block:: console
   116	
   117	    $ DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=my_postgres_settings tox -e py39-postgres
   118	
   119	Windows users should use:
   120	
   121	.. code-block:: doscon
   122	
   123	    ...\> set DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=my_postgres_settings
   124	    ...\> tox -e py39-postgres
   125	
   126	Running the JavaScript tests
   127	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   128	
   129	Django includes a set of :ref:`JavaScript unit tests <javascript-tests>` for
   130	functions in certain contrib apps. The JavaScript tests aren't run by default
   131	using ``tox`` because they require ``Node.js`` to be installed and aren't
   132	necessary for the majority of patches. To run the JavaScript tests using
   133	``tox``:
   134	
   135	.. console::
   136	
   137	    $ tox -e javascript
   138	
   139	This command runs ``npm install`` to ensure test requirements are up to
   140	date and then runs ``npm test``.
   141	
   142	Running tests using ``django-docker-box``
   143	-----------------------------------------
   144	
   145	`django-docker-box`_ allows you to run the Django's test suite across all
   146	supported databases and python versions. See the `django-docker-box`_ project
   147	page for installation and usage instructions.
   148	
   149	.. _django-docker-box: https://github.com/django/django-docker-box/
   150	
   151	.. _running-unit-tests-settings:
   152	
   153	Using another ``settings`` module
   154	---------------------------------
   155	
   156	The included settings module (``tests/test_sqlite.py``) allows you to run the
   157	test suite using SQLite. If you want to run the tests using a different
   158	database, you'll need to define your own settings file. Some tests, such as
   159	those for ``contrib.postgres``, are specific to a particular database backend
   160	and will be skipped if run with a different backend. Some tests are skipped or
   161	expected failures on a particular database backend (see
   162	``DatabaseFeatures.django_test_skips`` and
   163	``DatabaseFeatures.django_test_expected_failures`` on each backend).
   164	
   165	To run the tests with different settings, ensure that the module is on your
   166	:envvar:`PYTHONPATH` and pass the module with ``--settings``.
   167	
   168	The :setting:`DATABASES` setting in any test settings module needs to define
   169	two databases:
   170	
   171	* A ``default`` database. This database should use the backend that
   172	  you want to use for primary testing.
   173	
   174	* A database with the alias ``other``. The ``other`` database is used to test
   175	  that queries can be directed to different databases. This database should use
   176	  the same backend as the ``default``, and it must have a different name.
   177	
   178	If you're using a backend that isn't SQLite, you will need to provide other
   179	details for each database:
   180	
   181	* The :setting:`USER` option needs to specify an existing user account
   182	  for the database. That user needs permission to execute ``CREATE DATABASE``
   183	  so that the test database can be created.
   184	
   185	* The :setting:`PASSWORD` option needs to provide the password for
   186	  the :setting:`USER` that has been specified.
   187	
   188	Test databases get their names by prepending ``test_`` to the value of the
   189	:setting:`NAME` settings for the databases defined in :setting:`DATABASES`.
   190	These test databases are deleted when the tests are finished.
   191	
   192	You will also need to ensure that your database uses UTF-8 as the default
   193	character set. If your database server doesn't use UTF-8 as a default charset,
   194	you will need to include a value for :setting:`CHARSET <TEST_CHARSET>` in the
   195	test settings dictionary for the applicable database.
   196	
   197	.. _runtests-specifying-labels:
   198	
   199	Running only some of the tests
   200	------------------------------
   201	
   202	Django's entire test suite takes a while to run, and running every single test
   203	could be redundant if, say, you just added a test to Django that you want to
   204	run quickly without running everything else. You can run a subset of the unit
   205	tests by appending the names of the test modules to ``runtests.py`` on the
   206	command line.
   207	
   208	For example, if you'd like to run tests only for generic relations and
   209	internationalization, type:
   210	
   211	.. console::
   212	
   213	   $ ./runtests.py --settings=path.to.settings generic_relations i18n
   214	
   215	How do you find out the names of individual tests? Look in ``tests/`` — each
   216	directory name there is the name of a test.
   217	
   218	If you want to run only a particular class of tests, you can specify a list of
   219	paths to individual test classes. For example, to run the ``TranslationTests``
   220	of the ``i18n`` module, type:
   221	
   222	.. console::
   223	
   224	   $ ./runtests.py --settings=path.to.settings i18n.tests.TranslationTests
   225	
   226	Going beyond that, you can specify an individual test method like this:
   227	
   228	.. console::
   229	
   230	   $ ./runtests.py --settings=path.to.settings i18n.tests.TranslationTests.test_lazy_objects
   231	
   232	You can run tests starting at a specified top-level module with ``--start-at``
   233	option. For example:
   234	
   235	.. console::
   236	
   237	   $ ./runtests.py --start-at=wsgi
   238	
   239	You can also run tests starting after a specified top-level module with
   240	``--start-after`` option. For example:
   241	
   242	.. console::
   243	
   244	   $ ./runtests.py --start-after=wsgi
   245	
   246	Note that the ``--reverse`` option doesn't impact on ``--start-at`` or
   247	``--start-after`` options. Moreover these options cannot be used with test
   248	labels.
   249	
   250	Running the Selenium tests
   251	--------------------------
   252	
   253	Some tests require Selenium and a web browser. To run these tests, you must
   254	install the :pypi:`selenium` package and run the tests with the
   255	``--selenium=<BROWSERS>`` option. For example, if you have Firefox and Google
   256	Chrome installed:
   257	
   258	.. console::
   259	
   260	   $ ./runtests.py --selenium=firefox,chrome
   261	
   262	See the `selenium.webdriver`_ package for the list of available browsers.
   263	
   264	Specifying ``--selenium`` automatically sets ``--tags=selenium`` to run only
   265	the tests that require selenium.
   266	
   267	Some browsers (e.g. Chrome or Firefox) support headless testing, which can be
   268	faster and more stable. Add the ``--headless`` option to enable this mode.
   269	
   270	.. _selenium.webdriver: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/selenium/tree/trunk/py/selenium/webdriver
   271	
   272	.. _running-unit-tests-dependencies:
   273	
   274	Running all the tests
   275	---------------------
   276	
   277	If you want to run the full suite of tests, you'll need to install a number of
   278	dependencies:
   279	
   280	* :pypi:`aiosmtpd`
   281	* :pypi:`argon2-cffi` 19.2.0+
   282	* :pypi:`asgiref` 3.6.0+ (required)
   283	* :pypi:`bcrypt`
   284	* :pypi:`colorama`
   285	* :pypi:`docutils`
   286	* :pypi:`geoip2`
   287	* :pypi:`Jinja2` 2.11+
   288	* :pypi:`numpy`
   289	* :pypi:`Pillow` 6.2.1+
   290	* :pypi:`PyYAML`
   291	* :pypi:`pytz` (required)
   292	* :pypi:`pywatchman`
   293	* :pypi:`redis` 3.4+
   294	* :pypi:`setuptools`
   295	* :pypi:`memcached`, plus a `supported Python binding
   296	  <https://memcached.org/>`_
   297	* `gettext <https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/manual/gettext.html>`_
   298	  (:ref:`gettext_on_windows`)
   299	* :pypi:`selenium`
   300	* :pypi:`sqlparse` 0.3.1+ (required)
   301	* :pypi:`tblib` 1.5.0+
   302	
   303	You can find these dependencies in `pip requirements files
   304	<https://pip.pypa.io/en/latest/user_guide/#requirements-files>`_ inside the
   305	``tests/requirements`` directory of the Django source tree and install them
   306	like so:
   307	
   308	.. console::
   309	
   310	   $ python -m pip install -r tests/requirements/py3.txt
   311	
   312	If you encounter an error during the installation, your system might be missing
   313	a dependency for one or more of the Python packages. Consult the failing
   314	package's documentation or search the web with the error message that you
   315	encounter.
   316	
   317	You can also install the database adapter(s) of your choice using
   318	``oracle.txt``, ``mysql.txt``, or ``postgres.txt``.
   319	
   320	If you want to test the memcached or Redis cache backends, you'll also need to
   321	define a :setting:`CACHES` setting that points at your memcached or Redis
   322	instance respectively.
   323	
   324	To run the GeoDjango tests, you will need to :doc:`set up a spatial database
   325	and install the Geospatial libraries</ref/contrib/gis/install/index>`.
   326	
   327	Each of these dependencies is optional. If you're missing any of them, the
   328	associated tests will be skipped.
   329	
   330	To run some of the autoreload tests, you'll need to install the
   331	`Watchman <https://facebook.github.io/watchman/>`_ service.
   332	
   333	Code coverage
   334	-------------
   335	
   336	Contributors are encouraged to run coverage on the test suite to identify areas
   337	that need additional tests. The coverage tool installation and use is described
   338	in :ref:`testing code coverage<topics-testing-code-coverage>`.
   339	
   340	Coverage should be run in a single process to obtain accurate statistics. To
   341	run coverage on the Django test suite using the standard test settings:
   342	
   343	.. console::
   344	
   345	   $ coverage run ./runtests.py --settings=test_sqlite --parallel=1
   346	
   347	After running coverage, generate the html report by running:
   348	
   349	.. console::
   350	
   351	   $ coverage html
   352	
   353	When running coverage for the Django tests, the included ``.coveragerc``
   354	settings file  defines ``coverage_html`` as the output directory for the report
   355	and also excludes several directories not relevant to the results
   356	(test code or external code included in Django).
   357	
   358	.. _contrib-apps:
   359	
   360	Contrib apps
   361	============
   362	
   363	Tests for contrib apps can be found in the :source:`tests/` directory, typically
   364	under ``<app_name>_tests``. For example, tests for ``contrib.auth`` are located
   365	in :source:`tests/auth_tests`.
   366	
   367	.. _troubleshooting-unit-tests:
   368	
   369	Troubleshooting
   370	===============
   371	
   372	Test suite hangs or shows failures on ``main`` branch
   373	-----------------------------------------------------
   374	
   375	Ensure you have the latest point release of a :ref:`supported Python version
   376	<faq-python-version-support>`, since there are often bugs in earlier versions
   377	that may cause the test suite to fail or hang.
   378	
   379	On **macOS** (High Sierra and newer versions), you might see this message
   380	logged, after which the tests hang:
   381	
   382	.. code-block:: pytb
   383	
   384	    objc[42074]: +[__NSPlaceholderDate initialize] may have been in progress in
   385	    another thread when fork() was called.
   386	
   387	To avoid this set a ``OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY`` environment
   388	variable, for example:
   389	
   390	.. code-block:: shell
   391	
   392	    $ OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY=YES ./runtests.py
   393	
   394	Or add ``export OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY=YES`` to your shell's
   395	startup file (e.g. ``~/.profile``).
   396	
   397	Many test failures with ``UnicodeEncodeError``
   398	----------------------------------------------
   399	
   400	If the ``locales`` package is not installed, some tests will fail with a
   401	``UnicodeEncodeError``.
   402	
   403	You can resolve this on Debian-based systems, for example, by running:
   404	
   405	.. code-block:: console
   406	
   407	    $ apt-get install locales
   408	    $ dpkg-reconfigure locales
   409	
   410	You can resolve this for macOS systems by configuring your shell's locale:
   411	
   412	.. code-block:: console
   413	
   414	    $ export LANG="en_US.UTF-8"
   415	    $ export LC_ALL="en_US.UTF-8"
   416	
   417	Run the ``locale`` command to confirm the change. Optionally, add those export
   418	commands to your shell's startup file (e.g. ``~/.bashrc`` for Bash) to avoid
   419	having to retype them.
   420	
   421	Tests that only fail in combination
   422	-----------------------------------
   423	
   424	In case a test passes when run in isolation but fails within the whole suite,
   425	we have some tools to help analyze the problem.
   426	
   427	The ``--bisect`` option of ``runtests.py`` will run the failing test while
   428	halving the test set it is run together with on each iteration, often making
   429	it possible to identify a small number of tests that may be related to the
   430	failure.
   431	
   432	For example, suppose that the failing test that works on its own is
   433	``ModelTest.test_eq``, then using:
   434	
   435	.. console::
   436	
   437	    $ ./runtests.py --bisect basic.tests.ModelTest.test_eq
   438	
   439	will try to determine a test that interferes with the given one. First, the
   440	test is run with the first half of the test suite. If a failure occurs, the
   441	first half of the test suite is split in two groups and each group is then run
   442	with the specified test. If there is no failure with the first half of the test
   443	suite, the second half of the test suite is run with the specified test and
   444	split appropriately as described earlier. The process repeats until the set of
   445	failing tests is minimized.
   446	
   447	The ``--pair`` option runs the given test alongside every other test from the
   448	suite, letting you check if another test has side-effects that cause the

# Missing AdminReadonlyField.contents() Method Implementation

## Problem Summary

The `AdminReadonlyField` class in `django/contrib/admin/helpers.py` is missing its `contents()` method implementation. This method is essential for rendering readonly field values in Django admin forms and is called by admin templates (`admin/includes/fieldset.html` and `admin/edit_inline/tabular.html`) via `{{ field.contents }}`.

## Current Impact

Without the `contents()` method, readonly fields in Django admin forms cannot display their values properly. This affects:

- Regular admin change forms where readonly fields are displayed
- Inline admin forms with readonly fields  
- Any custom admin interface that relies on readonly field rendering

The missing method would cause `AttributeError` exceptions when admin templates attempt to access `field.contents` for readonly field instances.

The `contents()` method should return a properly formatted and escaped string representation of the readonly field's value. The method needs to:

1. Handle field lookup and value retrieval using the `lookup_field` utility function

The implementation should integrate seamlessly with Django's admin field rendering system and maintain compatibility with existing admin templates and functionality.

    TestRunner = get_runner(settings)

    test_runner = TestRunner(
        verbosity=verbosity,
        interactive=interactive,

    with warnings.catch_warnings():

    return failures


def bisect_tests(bisection_label, options, test_labels):
    state = setup(int(options.verbosity), test_labels)

    test_labels = test_labels or get_installed()

    print('***** Bisecting test suite: %s' % ' '.join(test_labels))

    # Make sure the bisection point isn't in the test list
    # Also remove tests that need to be run in specific combinations
    for label in [bisection_label, 'model_inheritance_same_model_name']:
        try:
            test_labels.remove(label)
        except ValueError:
            pass

    subprocess_args = [
        sys.executable, upath(__file__), '--settings=%s' % options.settings]
    if options.failfast:
        subprocess_args.append('--failfast')
    if options.verbosity:
        subprocess_args.append('--verbosity=%s' % options.verbosity)
    if not options.interactive:
        subprocess_args.append('--noinput')

    iteration = 1
    while len(test_labels) > 1:
        midpoint = len(test_labels) // 2
        test_labels_a = test_labels[:midpoint] + [bisection_label]
        test_labels_b = test_labels[midpoint:] + [bisection_label]
        print('***** Pass %da: Running the first half of the test suite' % iteration)
        print('***** Test labels: %s' % ' '.join(test_labels_a))
        failures_a = subprocess.call(subprocess_args + test_labels_a)

        print('***** Pass %db: Running the second half of the test suite' % iteration)
        print('***** Test labels: %s' % ' '.join(test_labels_b))
        print('')
        failures_b = subprocess.call(subprocess_args + test_labels_b)

        if failures_a and not failures_b:
            print("***** Problem found in first half. Bisecting again...")
            iteration = iteration + 1
            test_labels = test_labels_a[:-1]
        elif failures_b and not failures_a:
            print("***** Problem found in second half. Bisecting again...")
            iteration = iteration + 1
            test_labels = test_labels_b[:-1]
        elif failures_a and failures_b:
            print("***** Multiple sources of failure found")
            break
        else:
            print("***** No source of failure found... try pair execution (--pair)")
            break

    if len(test_labels) == 1:
        print("***** Source of error: %s" % test_labels[0])
    teardown(state)


def paired_tests(paired_test, options, test_labels):
    state = setup(int(options.verbosity), test_labels)

    test_labels = test_labels or get_installed()

    print('***** Trying paired execution')

    # Make sure the constant member of the pair isn't in the test list
    # Also remove tests that need to be run in specific combinations
    for label in [paired_test, 'model_inheritance_same_model_name']:
        try:
            test_labels.remove(label)
        except ValueError:
            pass

    subprocess_args = [
        sys.executable, upath(__file__), '--settings=%s' % options.settings]
    if options.failfast:
        subprocess_args.append('--failfast')
    if options.verbosity:
        subprocess_args.append('--verbosity=%s' % options.verbosity)
    if not options.interactive:
        subprocess_args.append('--noinput')

    for i, label in enumerate(test_labels):
        print('***** %d of %d: Check test pairing with %s' % (
              i + 1, len(test_labels), label))
        failures = subprocess.call(subprocess_args + [label, paired_test])
        if failures:
            print('***** Found problem pair with %s' % label)
            return

    print('***** No problem pair found')
    teardown(state)

import os

from django.db import models
from django.db.models.sql.query import Query
from tests.models import Author, Book

def test_set_values_basic():
    """Test basic set_values functionality."""
    print("Test 1: Basic set_values with field names...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.set_values(['name', 'email'])
    assert query.has_select_fields == True
    assert query.values_select == ('name', 'email')
    assert query.default_cols == False
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_empty():
    """Test set_values with empty fields list."""
    print("Test 2: set_values with empty fields list...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.set_values([])
    assert query.has_select_fields == True
    assert query.values_select == tuple(f.attname for f in Author._meta.concrete_fields)
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_with_extra():
    """Test set_values with extra select fields."""
    print("Test 3: set_values with extra select fields...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.extra['full_name'] = ('CONCAT(firstname, " ", lastname)', [])
    query.set_values(['name', 'full_name'])
    assert query.has_select_fields == True
    assert 'full_name' in query.extra_select_mask
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_with_annotation():
    """Test set_values with annotation fields."""
    print("Test 4: set_values with annotation fields...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.annotations['total_books'] = models.Count('book')
    query.set_values(['name', 'total_books'])
    assert query.has_select_fields == True
    assert 'total_books' in query.annotation_select_mask
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_select_related_false():
    """Test that set_values sets select_related to False."""
    print("Test 5: set_values sets select_related to False...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.select_related = True
    query.set_values(['name'])
    assert query.select_related == False
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_clears_deferred_loading():
    """Test that set_values clears deferred loading."""
    print("Test 6: set_values clears deferred loading...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.deferred_loading = (frozenset(['name']), False)
    query.set_values(['email'])
    assert query.deferred_loading == (frozenset(), True)
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_clears_select_fields():
    """Test that set_values clears select fields."""
    print("Test 7: set_values clears select fields...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.select = (models.F('name'),)
    query.set_values(['email'])
    assert query.select == ()
    assert query.values_select == ('email',)
    print("  PASSED")

def test_set_values_with_group_by():
    """Test set_values with existing GROUP BY."""
    print("Test 8: set_values with existing GROUP BY...")
    query = Query(Author)
    query.group_by = (models.F('name'),)
    query.set_values(['email'])
    assert query.group_by is not None
    print("  PASSED")

"""
Test for the set_values method using Django's test framework.
"""
import os
import sys
import django

# Setup Django
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'test_sqlite')
sys.path.insert(0, '/project')
sys.path.insert(0, '/project/tests')

django.setup()

from django.test import TestCase
from django.db import models
from django.db.models.sql.query import Query
from tests.expressions.models import Company, Employee


class SetValuesTests(TestCase):
    """Test the set_values method on Query class."""
    
    def test_set_values_basic(self):
        """Test basic set_values functionality."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.set_values(['name', 'num_employees'])
        self.assertTrue(query.has_select_fields)
        self.assertEqual(query.values_select, ('name', 'num_employees'))
        self.assertFalse(query.default_cols)
    
    def test_set_values_empty(self):
        """Test set_values with empty fields list."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.set_values([])
        self.assertTrue(query.has_select_fields)
        self.assertEqual(
            query.values_select,
            tuple(f.attname for f in Company._meta.concrete_fields)
        )
    
    def test_set_values_with_extra(self):
        """Test set_values with extra select fields."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.extra['full_name'] = ('CONCAT(name, " Inc.")', [])
        query.set_values(['name', 'full_name'])
        self.assertTrue(query.has_select_fields)
        self.assertIn('full_name', query.extra_select_mask)
    
    def test_set_values_with_annotation(self):
        """Test set_values with annotation fields."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.annotations['total_employees'] = models.Count('employee')
        query.set_values(['name', 'total_employees'])
        self.assertTrue(query.has_select_fields)
        self.assertIn('total_employees', query.annotation_select_mask)
    
    def test_set_values_select_related_false(self):
        """Test that set_values sets select_related to False."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.select_related = True
        query.set_values(['name'])
        self.assertFalse(query.select_related)
    
    def test_set_values_clears_deferred_loading(self):
        """Test that set_values clears deferred loading."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.deferred_loading = (frozenset(['name']), False)
        query.set_values(['num_employees'])
        self.assertEqual(query.deferred_loading, (frozenset(), True))
    
    def test_set_values_clears_select_fields(self):
        """Test that set_values clears select fields."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.select = (models.F('name'),)
        query.set_values(['num_employees'])
        self.assertEqual(query.select, ())
        self.assertEqual(query.values_select, ('num_employees',))
    
    def test_set_values_with_group_by(self):
        """Test set_values with existing GROUP BY."""
        query = Query(Company)
        query.group_by = (models.F('name'),)
        query.set_values(['num_employees'])
        self.assertIsNotNone(query.group_by)


if __name__ == '__main__':

    test_runner = TestRunner(verbosity=2, interactive=False, keepdb=False)

    sys.exit(bool(failures))

from django.test import TestCase
from django.db import models
from tests.expressions.models import Company, Employee


class IntegrationTest(TestCase):
    """Test that values() and values_list() work correctly."""
    
    @classmethod
    def setUpTestData(cls):
        cls.company1 = Company.objects.create(
            name="Example Inc.",
            num_employees=2300,
            num_chairs=5,
        )
        cls.company2 = Company.objects.create(
            name="Foobar Ltd.",
            num_employees=3,
            num_chairs=4,
        )
    
    def test_values_basic(self):
        """Test basic values() call."""
        result = Company.objects.values('name', 'num_employees')
        self.assertEqual(len(result), 2)
        names = [item['name'] for item in result]
        self.assertIn('Example Inc.', names)
        self.assertIn('Foobar Ltd.', names)
    
    def test_values_list_basic(self):
        """Test basic values_list() call."""
        result = Company.objects.values_list('name', 'num_employees')
        self.assertEqual(len(result), 2)
        names = [item[0] for item in result]
        self.assertIn('Example Inc.', names)
        self.assertIn('Foobar Ltd.', names)
    
    def test_values_with_annotation(self):
        """Test values() with annotation."""
        result = Company.objects.annotate(
            total_employees=models.Count('employee')
        ).values('name', 'total_employees')
        self.assertEqual(len(result), 2)
    
    def test_values_list_with_flat(self):
        """Test values_list() with flat=True."""
        result = Company.objects.values_list('name', flat=True)
        self.assertEqual(len(result), 2)
        names = list(result)
        self.assertIn('Example Inc.', names)
        self.assertIn('Foobar Ltd.', names)

class URLValidator(RegexValidator):
    ul = '\u00a1-\uffff'  # Unicode letters range (must not be a raw string).

    # IP patterns
    ipv4_re = r'(?:0|25[0-5]|2[0-4]\d|1\d?\d?|[1-9]\d?)(?:\.(?:0|25[0-5]|2[0-4]\d|1\d?\d?|[1-9]\d?)){3}'
    ipv6_re = r'\[[0-9a-f:.]+\]'  # (simple regex, validated later)

    # Host patterns
    hostname_re = r'[a-z' + ul + r'0-9](?:[a-z' + ul + r'0-9-]{0,61}[a-z' + ul + r'0-9])?'
    # Max length for domain name labels is 63 characters per RFC 1034 sec. 3.1
    domain_re = r'(?:\.(?!-)[a-z' + ul + r'0-9-]{1,63}(?<!-))*'
    tld_re = (
        r'\.'                                # dot
        r'(?!-)'                             # can't start with a dash
        r'(?:[a-z' + ul + '-]{2,63}'         # domain label
        r'|xn--[a-z0-9]{1,59})'              # or punycode label
        r'(?<!-)'                            # can't end with a dash
        r'\.?'                               # may have a trailing dot
    )
    host_re = '(' + hostname_re + domain_re + tld_re + '|localhost)'

    regex = _lazy_re_compile(
        r'^(?:[a-z0-9.+-]*)://'  # scheme is validated separately
        r'(?:[^\s:@/]+(?::[^\s:@/]*)?@)?'  # user:pass authentication
        r'(?:' + ipv4_re + '|' + ipv6_re + '|' + host_re + ')'
        r'(?::\d{2,5})?'  # port
        r'(?:[/?#][^\s]*)?'  # resource path
        r'\Z', re.IGNORECASE)
    message = _('Enter a valid URL.')
    schemes = ['http', 'https', 'ftp', 'ftps']
    unsafe_chars = frozenset('\t\r\n')
    max_length = 2048

    def __init__(self, schemes=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        if schemes is not None:
            self.schemes = schemes

    def __call__(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str) or len(value) > self.max_length:
            raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})
        if self.unsafe_chars.intersection(value):
            raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})
        # Check if the scheme is valid.
        scheme = value.split('://')[0].lower()
        if scheme not in self.schemes:
            raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})

        # Then check full URL
        try:
            super().__call__(value)
        except ValidationError as e:
            # Trivial case failed. Try for possible IDN domain
            if value:
                try:
                    scheme, netloc, path, query, fragment = urlsplit(value)
                except ValueError:  # for example, "Invalid IPv6 URL"
                    raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})
                try:
                    netloc = punycode(netloc)  # IDN -> ACE
                except UnicodeError:  # invalid domain part
                    raise e
                url = urlunsplit((scheme, netloc, path, query, fragment))
                super().__call__(url)
            else:
                raise
        else:
            # Now verify IPv6 in the netloc part
            host_match = re.search(r'^\[(.+)\](?::\d{2,5})?$', urlsplit(value).netloc)
            if host_match:
                potential_ip = host_match[1]
                try:
                    validate_ipv6_address(potential_ip)
                except ValidationError:
                    raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})

        # The maximum length of a full host name is 253 characters per RFC 1034
        # section 3.1. It's defined to be 255 bytes or less, but this includes
        # one byte for the length of the name and one byte for the trailing dot
        # that's used to indicate absolute names in DNS.
        if len(urlsplit(value).hostname) > 253:
            raise ValidationError(self.message, code=self.code, params={'value': value})

+    # Chrome will still consider example.com to be the hostname, so we must not
+    # allow this syntax.

   158	def base36_to_int(s):
   159	    """
   160	    Converts a base 36 string to an ``int``. Raises ``ValueError` if the
   161	    input won't fit into an int.
   162	    """
   163	    # To prevent overconsumption of server resources, reject any
   164	    # base36 string that is long than 13 base36 digits (13 digits
   165	    # is sufficient to base36-encode any 64-bit integer)
   166	    if len(s) > 13:
   167	        raise ValueError("Base36 input too large")
   168	    value = int(s, 36)
   169	    # ... then do a final check that the value will fit into an int to avoid
   170	    # returning a long (#15067). The long type was removed in Python 3.
   171	    if six.PY2 and value > sys.maxint:
   172	        raise ValueError("Base36 input too large")
   173	    return value

   175	def int_to_base36(i):
   176	    """
   177	    Converts an integer to a base36 string
   178	    """
   179	    digits = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
   180	    factor = 0
   181	    if i < 0:
   182	        raise ValueError("Negative base36 conversion input.")
   183	    if six.PY2:
   184	        if not isinstance(i, six.integer_types):
   185	            raise TypeError("Non-integer base36 conversion input.")
   186	        if i > sys.maxint:
   187	            raise ValueError("Base36 conversion input too large.")
   188	    # Find starting factor
   189	    while True:
   190	        factor += 1
   191	        if i < 36 ** factor:
   192	            factor -= 1
   193	            break
   194	    base36 = []
   195	    # Construct base36 representation
   196	    while factor >= 0:
   197	        j = 36 ** factor
   198	        base36.append(digits[i // j])
   199	        i = i % j
   200	        factor -= 1
   201	    return ''.join(base36)

   204	    """

   213	    might have been stripped.

   215	    s = s.encode('utf-8') # base64encode should only return ASCII.
   216	    try:
   217	        return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s.ljust(len(s) + len(s) % 4, b'='))

def is_safe_url(url, host=None):
    """
    Return ``True`` if the url is a safe redirection (i.e. it doesn't point to
    a different host and uses a safe scheme).

    Always returns ``False`` on an empty url.
    """
    if not url:
        return False
    # Chrome treats \ completely as /
    url = url.replace('\\', '/')
    # Chrome considers any URL with more than two slashes to be absolute, but
    # urlaprse is not so flexible. Treat any url with three slashes as unsafe.
    if url.startswith('///'):
        return False
    url_info = urlparse(url)
    # Forbid URLs like http:///example.com - with a scheme, but without a hostname.
    # In that URL, example.com is not the hostname but, a path component. However,
    # Chrome will still consider example.com to be the hostname, so we must not
    # allow this syntax.
    if not url_info.netloc and url_info.scheme:
        return False
    return (not url_info.netloc or url_info.netloc == host) and \
        (not url_info.scheme or url_info.scheme in ['http', 'https'])

def is_safe_url(url, host=None):
    """
    Return ``True`` if the url is a safe redirection (i.e. it doesn't point to
    a different host and uses a safe scheme).

    Always returns ``False`` on an empty url.

    if not url:
        return False
    # Chrome treats \ completely as /
    url = url.replace('\\', '/')
    # Chrome considers any URL with more than two slashes to be absolute, but
    # urlaprse is not so flexible. Treat any url with three slashes as unsafe.
    if url.startswith('///'):

    # allow this syntax.

        return False

+    as the provided language codes are taken from the HTTP request. See also
+    <https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2007/oct/26/security-fix/>.

+        return False

+        lang_code is not None
+        and lang_code in get_languages()
+        and check_for_language(lang_code)
+    ):

+    except LookupError:

+def _parse_accept_lang_header(lang_string):

+    Parse the lang_string, which is the body of an HTTP Accept-Language

+    Return an empty tuple if there are any format errors in lang_string.
+    """
+    result = []
+    pieces = accept_language_re.split(lang_string.lower())
+    if pieces[-1]:
+        return ()
+    for i in range(0, len(pieces) - 1, 3):
+        first, lang, priority = pieces[i : i + 3]
+        if first:
+            return ()
+        if priority:
+            priority = float(priority)
+        else:
+            priority = 1.0
+        result.append((lang, priority))
+    result.sort(key=lambda k: k[1], reverse=True)
+    return tuple(result)

+def parse_accept_lang_header(lang_string):
+    """
+    Parse the value of the Accept-Language header up to a maximum length.

+    denial of service and memory exhaustion attacks. Excessive memory could be
+    used if the raw value is very large as it would be cached due to the use of
+    functools.lru_cache() to avoid repetitive parsing of common header values.
+    """
+    # If the header value doesn't exceed the maximum allowed length, parse it.
+    if len(lang_string) <= ACCEPT_LANGUAGE_HEADER_MAX_LENGTH:
+        return _parse_accept_lang_header(lang_string)

+    # If there is at least one comma in the value, parse up to the last comma
+    # before the max length, skipping any truncated parts at the end of the
+    # header value.
+    if (index := lang_string.rfind(",", 0, ACCEPT_LANGUAGE_HEADER_MAX_LENGTH)) > 0:

+

+    # longer than the maximum allowed length and so truncated.
+    return ()

        # Optional "q=1.00", "q=0.8"
        (?:\s*;\s*q=(0(?:\.[0-9]{,3})?|1(?:\.0{,3})?))?
        # Multiple accepts per header.
        (?:\s*,\s*|$)

    re.VERBOSE,
)

    r"^[a-z]{1,8}(?:-[a-z0-9]{1,8})*(?:@[a-z0-9]{1,20})?$", re.IGNORECASE

language_code_prefix_re = _lazy_re_compile(r"^/(\w+([@-]\w+){0,2})(/|$)")"}

--- **Documentation**: [https://www.starlette.io/](https://www.starlette.io/) --- # Starlette Starlette is a lightweight [ASGI][asgi] framework/toolkit, which is ideal for building async web services in Python. It is production-ready, and gives you the following: * A lightweight, low-complexity HTTP web framework. * WebSocket support. * In-process background tasks. * Startup and shutdown events. * Test client built on `httpx`. * CORS, GZip, Static Files, Streaming responses. * Session and Cookie support. * 100% test coverage. * 100% type annotated codebase. * Few hard dependencies. * Compatible with `asyncio` and `trio` backends. * Great overall performance [against independent benchmarks][techempower]. ## Requirements Python 3.7+ (For Python 3.6 support, install version 0.19.1) ## Installation ```shell $ pip3 install starlette ```

    13	Introduction
    14	------------
    15	
    16	Flask-Admin is a batteries-included, simple-to-use `Flask <http://flask.pocoo.org/>`_ extension that lets you
    17	add admin interfaces to Flask applications. It is inspired by the *django-admin* package, but implemented in such
    18	a way that the developer has total control of the look, feel and functionality of the resulting application.
    19	
    20	Out-of-the-box, Flask-Admin plays nicely with various ORM's, including
    21	
    22	- `SQLAlchemy <http://www.sqlalchemy.org/>`_,
    23	
    24	- `MongoEngine <http://mongoengine.org/>`_,
    25	
    26	- `pymongo <http://api.mongodb.org/python/current/>`_ and
    27	
    28	- `Peewee <https://github.com/coleifer/peewee>`_.
    29	
    30	It also boasts a simple file management interface and a `redis client <http://redis.io/>`_ console.
    31	
    32	The biggest feature of Flask-Admin is flexibility. It aims to provide a set of simple tools that can be used for
    33	building admin interfaces of any complexity. So, to start off with you can create a very simple application in no time,
    34	with auto-generated CRUD-views for each of your models. But then you can go further and customize those views & forms
    35	as the need arises.
    36	
    37	Flask-Admin is an active project, well-tested and production ready.

    39	Examples

    41	Several usage examples are included in the */examples* folder. Please add your own, or improve
    42	on the existing examples, and submit a *pull-request*.

    44	To run the examples in your local environment::
    45

    49	    cd flask-admin

22 23 # Gradio: Build Machine Learning Web Apps — in Python 24 25 Gradio is an open-source Python library that is used to build machine learning and data science demos and web applications. 26 27 With Gradio, you can quickly create a beautiful user interface around your machine learning models or data science workflow and let people "try it out" by dragging-and-dropping in their own images, 28 pasting text, recording their own voice, and interacting with your demo, all through the browser. 29 30 ![Interface montage](readme_files/header-image.jpg) 31 32 Gradio is useful for: 33 34 - **Demoing** your machine learning models for clients/collaborators/users/students. 35 36 - **Deploying** your models quickly with automatic shareable links and getting feedback on model performance. 37 38 - **Debugging** your model interactively during development using built-in manipulation and interpretation tools. 39 40 ## Quickstart 41 42 **Prerequisite**: Gradio requires Python 3.7 or higher, that's all! 43 44 ### What Does Gradio Do? 45 46 One of the *best ways to share* your machine learning model, API, or data science workflow with others is to create an **interactive app** that allows your users or colleagues to try out the demo in their browsers. 47 48 Gradio allows you to **build demos and share them, all in Python.** And usually in just a few lines of code! So let's get started. 49 50 ### Hello, World 51 52 To get Gradio running with a simple "Hello, World" example, follow these three steps: 53 54 1\. Install Gradio using pip: 55 56 ```bash 57 pip install gradio 58 ``` 59 60 2\. Run the code below as a Python script or in a Jupyter Notebook (or [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/18ODkJvyxHutTN0P5APWyGFO_xwNcgHDZ?usp=sharing)): 61 62 ```python 63 import gradio as gr 64 65 def greet(name): 66 return "Hello " + name + "!" 67 68 demo = gr.Interface(fn=greet, inputs="text", outputs="text") 69 70 demo.launch() 71 ``` 72 73 74 3\. The demo below will appear automatically within the Jupyter Notebook, or pop in a browser on [http://localhost:7860](http://localhost:7860) if running from a script: 75 76 ![`hello_world` demo](demo/hello_world/screenshot.gif) 77 78 When developing locally, if you want to run the code as a Python script, you can use the Gradio CLI to launch the application **in reload mode**, which will provide seamless and fast development. Learn more about reloading in the [Auto-Reloading Guide](https://gradio.app/developing-faster-with-reload-mode/). 79 80 ```bash 81 gradio app.py 82 ``` 83 84 Note: you can also do `python app.py`, but it won't provide the automatic reload mechanism. 85 86 ### The `Interface` Class 87 88 You'll notice that in order to make the demo, we created a `gradio.Interface`. This `Interface` class can wrap any Python function with a user interface. In the example above, we saw a simple text-based function, but the function could be anything from music generator to a tax calculator to the prediction function of a pretrained machine learning model. 89 90 The core `Interface` class is initialized with three required parameters: 91 92 - `fn`: the function to wrap a UI around 93 - `inputs`: which component(s) to use for the input (e.g. `"text"`, `"image"` or `"audio"`) 94 - `outputs`: which component(s) to use for the output (e.g. `"text"`, `"image"` or `"label"`) 95 96 Let's take a closer look at these components used to provide input and output. 97 98 ### Components Attributes 99 100 We saw some simple `Textbox` components in the previous examples, but what if you want to change how the UI components look or behave? 101 102 Let's say you want to customize the input text field — for example, you wanted it to be larger and have a text placeholder. If we use the actual class for `Textbox` instead of using the string shortcut, you have access to much more customizability through component attributes. 103 104 ```python 105 import gradio as gr 106 107 def greet(name): 108 return "Hello " + name + "!" 109 110 demo = gr.Interface( 111 fn=greet, 112 inputs=gr.Textbox(lines=2, placeholder="Name Here..."), 113 outputs="text", 114 ) 115 demo.launch() 116 ``` 117 118 ![`hello_world_2` demo](demo/hello_world_2/screenshot.gif) 119 120 ### Multiple Input and Output Components 121 122 Suppose you had a more complex function, with multiple inputs and outputs. In the example below, we define a function that takes a string, boolean, and number, and returns a string and number. Take a look how you pass a list of input and output components. 123 124 ```python 125 import gradio as gr 126 127 def greet(name, is_morning, temperature): 128 salutation = "Good morning" if is_morning else "Good evening" 129 greeting = f"{salutation} {name}. It is {temperature} degrees today" 130 celsius = (temperature - 32) * 5 / 9 131 return greeting, round(celsius, 2) 132 133 demo = gr.Interface( 134 fn=greet, 135 inputs=["text", "checkbox", gr.Slider(0, 100)], 136 outputs=["text", "number"], 137 ) 138 demo.launch() 139 ``` 140 141 ![`hello_world_3` demo](demo/hello_world_3/screenshot.gif) 142 143 You simply wrap the components in a list. Each component in the `inputs` list corresponds to one of the parameters of the function, in order. Each component in the `outputs` list corresponds to one of the values returned by the function, again in order. 144 145 ### An Image Example 146 147 Gradio supports many types of components, such as `Image`, `DataFrame`, `Video`, or `Label`. Let's try an image-to-image function to get a feel for these! 148 149 ```python 150 import numpy as np 151 import gradio as gr 152 153 def sepia(input_img): 154 sepia_filter = np.array([ 155 [0.393, 0.769, 0.189], 156 [0.349, 0.686, 0.168], 157 [0.272, 0.534, 0.131] 158 ]) 159 sepia_img = input_img.dot(sepia_filter.T) 160 sepia_img /= sepia_img.max() 161 return sepia_img 162 163 demo = gr.Interface(sepia, gr.Image(shape=(200, 200)), "image") 164 demo.launch() 165 ``` 166 167 ![`sepia_filter` demo](demo/sepia_filter/screenshot.gif) 168 169 When using the `Image` component as input, your function will receive a NumPy array with the shape `(height, width, 3)`, where the last dimension represents the RGB values. We'll return an image as well in the form of a NumPy array. 170 171 You can also set the datatype used by the component with the `type=` keyword argument. For example, if you wanted your function to take a file path to an image instead of a NumPy array, the input `Image` component could be written as: 172 173 ```python 174 gr.Image(type="filepath", shape=...) 175 ``` 176 177 Also note that our input `Image` component comes with an edit button 🖉, which allows for cropping and zooming into images. Manipulating images in this way can help reveal biases or hidden flaws in a machine learning model! 178 179 You can read more about the many components and how to use them in the [Gradio docs](https://gradio.app/docs). 180 181 ### Blocks: More Flexibility and Control 182 183 Gradio offers two classes to build apps: 184 185 1\. **Interface**, that provides a high-level abstraction for creating demos that we've been discussing so far. 186 187 2\. **Blocks**, a low-level API for designing web apps with more flexible layouts and data flows. Blocks allows you to do things like feature multiple data flows and demos, control where components appear on the page, handle complex data flows (e.g. outputs can serve as inputs to other functions), and update properties/visibility of components based on user interaction — still all in Python. If this customizability is what you need, try `Blocks` instead! 188 189 ### Hello, Blocks 190 191 Let's take a look at a simple example. Note how the API here differs from `Interface`. 192 193 ```python 194 import gradio as gr 195 196 def greet(name): 197 return "Hello " + name + "!" 198 199 with gr.Blocks() as demo: 200 name = gr.Textbox(label="Name") 201 output = gr.Textbox(label="Output Box") 202 greet_btn = gr.Button("Greet") 203 greet_btn.click(fn=greet, inputs=name, outputs=output) 204 205 demo.launch() 206 ``` 207 208 ![`hello_blocks` demo](demo/hello_blocks/screenshot.gif) 209 210 Things to note: 211 212 - `Blocks` are made with a `with` clause, and any component created inside this clause is automatically added to the app. 213 - Components appear vertically in the app in the order they are created. (Later we will cover customizing layouts!) 214 - A `Button` was created, and then a `click` event-listener was added to this button. The API for this should look familiar! Like an `Interface`, the `click` method takes a Python function, input components, and output components. 215 216 ### More Complexity 217 218 Here's an app to give you a taste of what's possible with `Blocks`: 219 220 ```python 221 import numpy as np 222 import gradio as gr 223 224 225 def flip_text(x): 226 return x[::-1] 227 228 229 def flip_image(x): 230 return np.fliplr(x) 231 232 233 with gr.Blocks() as demo: 234 gr.Markdown("Flip text or image files using this demo.") 235 with gr.Tab("Flip Text"): 236 text_input = gr.Textbox() 237 text_output = gr.Textbox() 238 text_button = gr.Button("Flip") 239 with gr.Tab("Flip Image"): 240 with gr.Row(): 241 image_input = gr.Image() 242 image_output = gr.Image() 243 image_button = gr.Button("Flip") 244 245 with gr.Accordion("Open for More!"): 246 gr.Markdown("Look at me...") 247 248 text_button.click(flip_text, inputs=text_input, outputs=text_output) 249 image_button.click(flip_image, inputs=image_input, outputs=image_output) 250 251 demo.launch() 252 ``` 253 254 ![`blocks_flipper` demo](demo/blocks_flipper/screenshot.gif) 255 256 A lot more going on here! We'll cover how to create complex `Blocks` apps like this in the [building with blocks](https://gradio.app/building_with_blocks) section for you. 257 258 Congrats, you're now familiar with the basics of Gradio! 🥳 Go to our [next guide](https://gradio.app/key_features) to learn more about the key features of Gradio. 259 260 261 ## Open Source Stack 262 263 Gradio is built with many wonderful open-source libraries, please support them as well! 264 265 [](https://huggingface.co) 266 [](https://www.python.org) 267 [](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com) 268 [](https://www.encode.io) 269 [](https://svelte.dev) 270 [](https://vitejs.dev) 271 [](https://pnpm.io) 272 [](https://tailwindcss.com) 273 274 ## License 275 276 Gradio is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 found in the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file in the root directory of this repository. 277 278 ## Citation 279 280 Also check out the paper *[Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02569), ICML HILL 2019*, and please cite it if you use Gradio in your work. 281 282 ``` 283 @article{abid2019gradio, 284 title = {Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild}, 285 author = {Abid, Abubakar and Abdalla, Ali and Abid, Ali and Khan, Dawood and Alfozan, Abdulrahman and Zou, James}, 286 journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.02569}, 287 year = {2019}, 288 } 289 ``` 290

        cls,
        config: dict,
        fns: list[Callable],
        root_url: str,
    ) -> Blocks:
        """
        Factory method that creates a Blocks from a config and list of functions. Used
        internally by the gradio.external.load() method.

        Parameters:
        config: a dictionary containing the configuration of the Blocks.
        fns: a list of functions that are used in the Blocks. Must be in the same order as the dependencies in the config.
        root_url: an external url to use as a root URL when serving files for components in the Blocks.

            for block_config in components_config:
                if block_config["id"] == id:
                    break
            else:

            cls = component_or_layout_class(block_config["type"])

   274	(and thus impersonate any user). How to do this varies by your chosen proxy,
   275	but generally involves configuring it to strip out headers that normalize to the
   276	same name as the chosen identity header.
   277	
   278	To enable this feature, set the `REMOTE_USER_HEADER` value to a header you wish to
   279	authenticate with. HTTP headers will be prefixed with `HTTP_` and have any dashes
   280	converted to underscores. Headers without that prefix can be set by the WSGI server
   281	itself only, which is more secure.
   282	
   283	When `REMOTE_USER_HEADER` is set, Healthchecks will:
   284	 - assume the header contains user's email address
   285	 - look up and automatically log in the user with a matching email address
   286	 - automatically create an user account if it does not exist
   287	 - disable the default authentication methods (login link to email, password)
   288	
   289	## External Object Storage
   290	
   291	Healthchecks can optionally store large ping bodies in S3-compatible object
   292	storage. To enable this feature, you will need to:
   293	
   294	* ensure you have the [MinIO Python library](https://docs.min.io/docs/python-client-quickstart-guide.html) installed:

   297	```
   298	* configure the credentials for accessing object storage: `S3_ACCESS_KEY`,
   299	  `S3_SECRET_KEY`, `S3_ENDPOINT`, `S3_REGION` and `S3_BUCKET`.
   300	
   301	Healthchecks will use external object storage for storing any request bodies that
   302	exceed 100 bytes. If the size of a request body is 100 bytes or below, Healthchecks
   303	will still store it in the database.

   305	Healthchecks automatically removes old stored ping bodies from object
   306	storage while uploading new data. However, Healthchecks does not automatically
   307	clean up data when you delete checks, projects or entire user accounts.

def _allow_redirect(redirect_url):
    if not redirect_url:
        return False

    parsed = urlparse(redirect_url)
    if parsed.netloc:
        # Allow redirects only to relative URLs
        return False

    try:
        match = resolve(parsed.path)
    except Resolver404:
        return False

    return match.url_name in POST_LOGIN_ROUTES


def _make_user(email, tz=None, with_project=True):
    username = str(uuid.uuid4())[:30]
    user = User(username=username, email=email)
    user.set_unusable_password()
    user.save()

    project = None
    if with_project:
        project = Project(owner=user)
        project.badge_key = user.username
        project.save()

        check = Check(project=project)
        check.set_name_slug("My First Check")
        check.save()

        channel = Channel(project=project)
        channel.kind = "email"
        channel.value = email
        channel.email_verified = True
        channel.save()

        channel.checks.add(check)

    # Ensure a profile gets created
    profile = Profile.objects.for_user(user)
    if tz:
        profile.tz = tz
        profile.save()

    return user


def _redirect_after_login(request):
    """Redirect to the URL indicated in ?next= query parameter."""

    redirect_url = request.GET.get("next")
    if _allow_redirect(redirect_url):
        return redirect(redirect_url)

    if request.user.project_set.count() == 1:
        project = request.user.project_set.first()
        return redirect("hc-checks", project.code)

    return redirect("hc-index")


def _check_2fa(request, user):
    have_keys = user.credentials.exists()
    profile = Profile.objects.for_user(user)
    if have_keys or profile.totp:
        # We have verified user's password or token, and now must
        # verify their security key. We store the following in user's session:
        # - user.id, to look up the user in the login_webauthn view
        # - user.email, to make sure email was not changed between the auth steps
        # - timestamp, to limit the max time between the auth steps
        request.session["2fa_user"] = [user.id, user.email, int(time.time())]

        if have_keys:
            path = reverse("hc-login-webauthn")
        else:
            path = reverse("hc-login-totp")

        redirect_url = request.GET.get("next")
        if _allow_redirect(redirect_url):
            path += "?next=%s" % redirect_url

        return redirect(path)

    auth_login(request, user)
    return _redirect_after_login(request)


def _new_key(nbytes=24):
    while True:
        candidate = token_urlsafe(nbytes)
        if candidate[0] not in "-_" and candidate[-1] not in "-_":
            return candidate


def login(request):
    form = forms.PasswordLoginForm()
    magic_form = forms.EmailLoginForm()

    if request.method == "POST":
        if request.POST.get("action") == "login":
            form = forms.PasswordLoginForm(request.POST)
            if form.is_valid():
                return _check_2fa(request, form.user)

        else:
            magic_form = forms.EmailLoginForm(request.POST)
            if magic_form.is_valid():
                redirect_url = request.GET.get("next")
                if not _allow_redirect(redirect_url):
                    redirect_url = None

                if magic_form.user:
                    profile = Profile.objects.for_user(magic_form.user)
                    profile.send_instant_login_link(redirect_url=redirect_url)

                response = redirect("hc-login-link-sent")
                # check_token looks for this cookie to decide if
                # it needs to do the extra POST step.
                response.set_cookie("auto-login", "1", max_age=300, httponly=True)
                return response

    if request.user.is_authenticated:
        return _redirect_after_login(request)

    bad_link = request.session.pop("bad_link", None)
    ctx = {
        "page": "login",
        "form": form,
        "magic_form": magic_form,
        "bad_link": bad_link,
        "registration_open": settings.REGISTRATION_OPEN,
        "support_email": settings.SUPPORT_EMAIL,
    }
    return render(request, "accounts/login.html", ctx)

    auth_logout(request)
    return redirect("hc-index")

   442	    temp_results: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[datetime, Credentials]] = {}
   443	
   444	    @callback
   445	    def store_result(client_id: str, result: Credentials) -> str:
   446	        """Store flow result and return a code to retrieve it."""
   447	        if not isinstance(result, Credentials):
   448	            raise TypeError("result has to be a Credentials instance")
   449	
   450	        code = uuid.uuid4().hex
   451	        temp_results[(client_id, code)] = (
   452	            dt_util.utcnow(),
   453	            result,
   454	        )
   455	        return code
   456	
   457	    @callback
   458	    def retrieve_result(client_id: str, code: str) -> Credentials | None:
   459	        """Retrieve flow result."""
   460	        key = (client_id, code)
   461	
   462	        if key not in temp_results:
   463	            return None
   464	
   465	        created, result = temp_results.pop(key)
   466	
   467	        # OAuth 4.2.1
   468	        # The authorization code MUST expire shortly after it is issued to
   469	        # mitigate the risk of leaks.  A maximum authorization code lifetime of
   470	        # 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED.
   471	        if dt_util.utcnow() - created < timedelta(minutes=10):
   472	            return result
   473	
   474	        return None
   475

[

# POST /auth/login_flow

Create a login flow. Will return the first step of the flow.

Pass in parameter 'client_id' and 'redirect_url' validate by indieauth.

Pass in parameter 'handler' to specify the auth provider to use. Auth providers
are identified by type and id.

And optional parameter 'type' has to set as 'link_user' if login flow used for
link credential to exist user. Default 'type' is 'authorize'.

{
    "client_id": "https://hassbian.local:8123/",
    "handler": ["local_provider", null],
    "redirect_url": "https://hassbian.local:8123/",

+class AuthProvidersView(HomeAssistantView):
+    """View to get available auth providers."""
+
+    url = "/auth/providers"
+    name = "api:auth:providers"
+    requires_auth = False
+
+    async def get(self, request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
+        """Get available auth providers."""
+        from homeassistant.components import onboarding
+        from homeassistant.components.person import DOMAIN as PERSON_DOMAIN
+        from homeassistant.helpers.network import is_cloud_connection
+
+        hass: HomeAssistant = request.app["hass"]
+
+        if not onboarding.async_is_user_onboarded(hass):
+            return self.json_message(
+                message="Onboarding not finished",
+                status_code=HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
+                message_code="onboarding_required",
+            )
+
+        providers = []
+        for provider in hass.auth.auth_providers:
+            if provider.type == "trusted_networks":
+                # Trusted networks provider is only available on local networks
+                if is_cloud_connection(hass):
+                    continue
+            elif provider.type == "homeassistant":
+                # Home Assistant provider is only available on local networks
+                if is_cloud_connection(hass):
+                    continue
+
+            provider_info = {
+                "name": provider.name,
+                "id": provider.id,
+                "type": provider.type,
+            }
+

+
+            providers.append(provider_info)
+

The aioxmpp XSO (XML Stream Object) processing system is missing several critical utility functions in `aioxmpp/xso/model.py` that are essential for XML parsing, event handling, and SAX conversion. These missing functions break the XSO parsing pipeline and prevent proper handling of unknown XML elements, event capture, and XML-to-SAX conversion.

## Missing Functionality

The following functions are currently missing from `aioxmpp.xso.model`:

1. **`drop_handler(ev_args)`** - A generator function that consumes and discards XML events for an entire element subtree by tracking element depth
2. **`enforce_unknown_child_policy(policy, ev_args, error_handler=None)`** - Enforces the configured policy for handling unknown child elements, either dropping them or raising errors
3. **`guard(dest, ev_args)`** - A protective wrapper that forwards events to a destination generator while handling exceptions and ensuring proper cleanup
4. **`lang_attr(instance, ctx)`** - A missing attribute handler that retrieves the `xml:lang` value from the parsing context
5. **`capture_events(receiver, dest)`** - A generator that captures all events sent to a receiver while maintaining transparent pass-through behavior
6. **`events_to_sax(events, dest)`** - Converts XSO event sequences to SAX events by calling appropriate SAX handler methods

## Impact

Without these functions:

- **XSO parsing fails** when encountering unknown child elements, as `enforce_unknown_child_policy` cannot determine whether to drop or fail on unknown content
- **CapturingXSO functionality is broken** since `capture_events` is required for event capture in the `CapturingXMLStreamClass.parse_events` method
- **XML language attribute inheritance doesn't work** as `lang_attr` is used as a missing handler for `xml:lang` attributes throughout the codebase
- **SAX conversion is unavailable** preventing conversion of captured XSO events back to SAX format
- **Error handling and recovery mechanisms fail** due to missing `guard` function that provides exception safety
- **Element dropping functionality is non-functional** as `drop_handler` is the core mechanism for ignoring unwanted XML subtrees

## Expected Behavior

The implementation should provide:

- **Event-driven XML processing** using generator-based suspendable functions that process SAX-like events
- **Configurable unknown element handling** supporting both DROP and FAIL policies with optional error handler callbacks
- **Transparent event capture** that maintains identical behavior to direct receiver usage while capturing events
- **Robust exception handling** with proper cleanup and error propagation
- **Context-aware attribute resolution** for XML language inheritance
- **Bidirectional event conversion** between XSO events and SAX events

The functions must integrate seamlessly with the existing XSO parsing infrastructure and maintain compatibility with the established event format: `("event_type", *event_args)` where event types include "start", "end", and "text".

def drop_handler(ev_args):
    """
    Generator function that consumes and discards XML events for an entire
    element subtree by tracking element depth.

    This function is used to ignore unwanted XML elements and all their
    children. It tracks the nesting level of elements and only stops
    consuming events when the original element's end tag is encountered.

    :param ev_args: The arguments of the "start" event for the element to drop.
                    Format: ``(namespace, localname, attrs)``

    :yields: No values (consumes all events for the subtree)

    Example usage::

        # Drop all events for the <foo> element and its children
        yield from drop_handler((None, "foo", {}))
    """
    namespace, localname, attrs = ev_args
    depth = 1

    while True:
        ev_type, *ev_args = yield
        if ev_type == "start":
            depth += 1
        elif ev_type == "end":
            depth -= 1
            if depth == 0:
                break


def enforce_unknown_child_policy(policy, ev_args, error_handler=None):
    """
    Enforces the configured policy for handling unknown child elements.

    When an unknown child element is encountered (i.e., an element for which
    no descriptor can be found to parse it), this function determines whether
    to drop the element or raise an error based on the specified policy.

    :param policy: The policy to enforce (:class:`UnknownChildPolicy`)
    :param ev_args: The arguments of the "start" event for the unknown element.
                    Format: ``(namespace, localname, attrs)``
    :param error_handler: Optional callable that receives the error and can
                          suppress it by returning ``True``. If not provided,
                          the default behavior is to raise the error.

    :yields: The original event arguments if policy is DROP, or raises
             :class:`ValueError` if policy is FAIL

    :raises ValueError: If policy is FAIL and no error handler is provided
                        or if error handler returns False
    """
    if policy == UnknownChildPolicy.DROP:
        yield from drop_handler(ev_args)
    else:  # policy == UnknownChildPolicy.FAIL
        if error_handler and error_handler(None, ev_args, None):
            # Error was suppressed by handler
            yield from drop_handler(ev_args)
        else:
            raise ValueError(
                "unknown child element: {}".format((ev_args[0], ev_args[1]))
            )


def guard(dest, ev_args):
    """
    A protective wrapper that forwards events to a destination generator
    while handling exceptions and ensuring proper cleanup.

    This function provides exception safety for event processing. It catches
    exceptions during event forwarding and ensures that the destination
    generator is properly closed. If an exception occurs, it is re-raised
    after cleanup.

    :param dest: The destination generator to forward events to
    :param ev_args: The arguments of the "start" event for the element being
                    processed. Format: ``(namespace, localname, attrs)``

    :yields: The result from the destination generator

    :raises: Any exception raised by the destination generator
    """
    try:
        dest.send(ev_args)
        while True:
            ev_type, *ev_args = yield
            try:
                result = dest.send(ev_args)
            except StopIteration as e:
                if e.value is not None:
                    yield e.value
                return
            else:
                yield result
    finally:
        try:
            dest.close()
        except:
            pass


def lang_attr(instance, ctx):
    """
    A missing attribute handler that retrieves the ``xml:lang`` value from
    the parsing context.

    This function is used as the `missing` handler for :class:`LangAttr`
    descriptors. It retrieves the language value from the parsing context
    instead of from the element's attributes.

    :param instance: The XSO instance being parsed
    :param ctx: The parsing context containing the language information

    :returns: The language value from the context, or ``None`` if not found
    """
    return ctx.get("lang")


def capture_events(receiver, dest):
    """
    A generator that captures all events sent to a receiver while maintaining
    transparent pass-through behavior.

    This function wraps a receiver generator and captures all events sent to
    it in a destination list. The captured events are available in the
    `dest` list, while the receiver continues to process events normally.

    The function maintains identical behavior to direct receiver usage while
    capturing events for later inspection or processing.

    :param receiver: The receiver generator to wrap
    :param dest: A list to capture events into

    :yields: The result from the receiver generator

    :raises: Any exception raised by the receiver generator
    """
    try:
        result = receiver.send(None)
        if result is not None:
            dest.append(result)
        while True:
            ev_type, *ev_args = yield
            try:
                result = receiver.send(ev_args)
            except StopIteration as e:
                if e.value is not None:
                    dest.append(e.value)
                return
            else:
                dest.append(result)
    finally:
        try:
            receiver.close()
        except:
            pass


def events_to_sax(events, dest):
    """
    Converts XSO event sequences to SAX events by calling appropriate SAX
    handler methods.

    This function takes a sequence of XSO events and converts them to SAX
    events by calling the appropriate methods on the destination SAX handler.

    XSO events have the format: ``(event_type, *event_args)`` where
    event_type is one of "start", "end", or "text".

    :param events: A sequence of XSO events
    :param dest: The SAX handler to call methods on

    :raises: ValueError if an unknown event type is encountered
    """
    for event in events:
        if not event:
            continue
        ev_type = event[0]
        ev_args = event[1:]

        if ev_type == "start":
            namespace, localname, attrs = ev_args
            dest.startElementNS((namespace, localname), None, attrs)
        elif ev_type == "end":
            namespace, localname = ev_args
            dest.endElementNS((namespace, localname), None)
        elif ev_type == "text":
            text = ev_args[0]
            dest.characters(text)
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown event type: {}".format(ev_type))

        .. attribute:: enum_member

            The enumeration member to which the :attr:`xso_class` belongs.

            This allows to use XSOs and enumeration members more
            interchangeably; see :attr:`enum_member` for details.

        .. method:: to_xso

            Return the XSO itself.

            This allows to use XSOs and enumeration members more
            interchangeably; see :meth:`to_xso` for details.

    Example usage::

        class TagEnum(aioxmpp.xso.XSOEnumMixin, enum.Enum):
            X = ("uri:foo", "x")
            Y = ("uri:foo", "y")

        TagEnum.X.xso_class.enabled = aioxmpp.xso.Attr(
            "enabled",
            type_=aioxmpp.xso.Bool()
        )

    The :class:`TagEnum` members then have a :attr:`xso_class` attribute which
    is a *subclass* of :class:`~aioxmpp.xso.XSO` (**not** an instance of a
    subclass of :class:`~aioxmpp.xso.XSO`).

    The :attr:`xso_class` for :attr:`TagEnum.X` also supports the ``enabled``
    attribute (due to it being monkey-patched onto it), while the
    :attr:`xso_class` for :attr:`TagEnum.Y` does not. Thus, monkey-patching
    can be used to customize the individual XSO classes of the members.

    To use such an enum on a descriptor, the following syntax can be used::

        class Element(aioxmpp.xso.XSO):
            TAG = ("uri:foo", "parent")

            child = aioxmpp.xso.Child([
                member.xso_class
                for member in TagEnum
            ])

they belong. Code which is only interested in the enumeration member

    def to_xso(self):
        """
        A new instance of the :attr:`xso_class`.

        This method exists to make it easier to use the XSO objects and the
        enumeration members interchangeably. The XSO objects also have the
        :meth:`to_xso` method which just returns the XSO unmodified.

        Code which needs an XSO, but does not care about the data, can thus use
        the :meth:`to_xso` method to "coerce" either (enumeration members and
        instances of their XSO classes) into XSOs.
        """
        return self.xso_class()

        .. attribute:: enum_member

            The enumeration member to which the :attr:`xso_class` belongs.

            This allows to use XSOs and enumeration members more
            interchangeably; see :attr:`enum_member` for details.

        .. method:: to_xso

            Return the XSO itself.

            This allows to use XSOs and enumeration members more
            interchangeably; see :meth:`to_xso` for details.

    Example usage::

        class TagEnum(aioxmpp.xso.XSOEnumMixin, enum.Enum):
            X = ("uri:foo", "x")
            Y = ("uri:foo", "y")

        TagEnum.X.xso_class.enabled = aioxmpp.xso.Attr(
            "enabled",
            type_=aioxmpp.xso.Bool()
        )

    The :class:`TagEnum` members then have a :attr:`xso_class` attribute which
    is a *subclass* of :class:`~aioxmpp.xso.XSO` (**not** an instance of a
    subclass of :class:`~aioxmpp.xso.XSO`).

    The :attr:`xso_class` for :attr:`TagEnum.X` also supports the ``enabled``
    attribute (due to it being monkey-patched onto it), while the
    :attr:`xso_class` for :attr:`TagEnum.Y` does not. Thus, monkey-patching
    can be used to customize the individual XSO classes of the members.

    To use such an enum on a descriptor, the following syntax can be used::

        class Element(aioxmpp.xso.XSO):
            TAG = ("uri:foo", "parent")

            child = aioxmpp.xso.Child([
                member.xso_class
                for member in TagEnum
            ])
    """

    def __init__(self, namespace, localname):
        super().__init__()
        self.xso_class = self._create_class()

+        # * the Reference element must have a URI attribute
